hops.title: Your rods work hardest in the dark
hops.text: Most people assume that switching off the bedroom light gives their eyes a rest. Rods do the opposite. In darkness, a mouse rod is estimated to spend roughly 100 million ATP molecules every second, most of it pumping ions to restore the gradients that its open channels and steady glutamate release run down. In bright light that shuts those channels, its energy use falls by more than 75 percent. Fruit fly photoreceptors run the other way: light opens their channels, and their energy use climbs about fivefold. Your rods run up their largest energy bill when there is nothing to see.

sources.citation: Okawa H, Sampath AP, Laughlin SB, Fain GL. ATP consumption by mammalian rod photoreceptors in darkness and in light. Current Biology 18(24):1917-1921 (2008).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand switching off a bedside table lamp in a darkened bedroom.
image.caption: Open channels keep a rod's energy bill high in darkness; as light closes them, its ATP use falls.

hops.title: Spotted Appaloosa horses and the missing ON channel
hops.text: More than 25,000 years ago, someone painted dark-spotted white horses in Pech-Merle cave, France. Ancient DNA later showed that prehistoric European horses carried an allele associated with leopard spotting in modern Appaloosas, so the painters may well have been drawing real animals. The spotting comes from retroviral DNA inserted inside the gene for TRPM1, the channel that ON bipolar cells open when glutamate falls. TRPM1 also works in skin pigment cells. A horse with one copy gets spots and sees normally at night. A horse with two copies has few or no spots, retinal TRPM1 expression about 0.05 percent of normal, and night blindness.

sources.citation: Pruvost M, Bellone R, Benecke N, et al. Genotypes of predomestic horses match phenotypes painted in Paleolithic works of cave art. PNAS 108(46):18626-18630 (2011).

Bellone RR, Holl H, Setaluri V, et al. Evidence for a retroviral insertion in TRPM1 as the cause of congenital stationary night blindness and leopard complex spotting in the horse. PLoS ONE 8(10):e78280 (2013).

Bellone RR, Brooks SA, Sandmeyer L, et al. Differential gene expression of TRPM1, the potential cause of congenital stationary night blindness and coat spotting patterns (LP) in the Appaloosa horse. Genetics 179(4):1861-1870 (2008).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white Appaloosa horse with dark spots standing in a sunlit pasture.
image.caption: One copy of a TRPM1 insertion spots an Appaloosa's coat; two copies block the ON bipolar response to light.

hops.title: John Dalton's preserved eyes
hops.text: In 1794 the chemist John Dalton described a puzzle he shared with his brother: both confused scarlet with green and pink with blue. Dalton's explanation was that the fluid inside his eyes was tinted blue and soaked up longer wavelengths, so he left instructions for his eyes to be examined after his death. The fluid turned out to be perfectly clear. The eyes were kept anyway, and in 1995 geneticists extracted DNA from the preserved tissue. Dalton lacked the M-cone pigment. He was a dichromat, comparing two cone classes where most people compare three, and the difference lay in his cones, not his eye fluid.

sources.citation: Hunt DM, Dulai KS, Bowmaker JK, Mollon JD. The chemistry of John Dalton's color blindness. Science 267(5200):984-988 (1995).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An antique wooden desk with a clear glass lens, a blue glass bottle, and scarlet and green ribbons.
image.caption: Dalton blamed blue eye fluid; DNA from his preserved eyes showed he lacked the M-cone pigment.
